```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# REBUILT ON EVERY RENDER, for the reason given in build_stats_catalog.R: a

K <- mw_init_stats(root)
A <- K$dbacc
L <- K$leadlag

fig <- function(name) file.path(root, "docs", "figures", paste0(name, ".png"))
style_manuscript_table <- function(x, ..., align = NULL) {
  knitr::kable(x, row.names = FALSE, align = align, ...)
}

# Formatting helpers local to this manuscript. `pc` prints a percentage the
# way the journal sets them; `cnt` a count with thousands separators.
# The cohort denominators, taken from the catalog where it carries them and
# from the frozen linkage manifest otherwise, never typed.
# Named exactly as build_stats_catalog.R defines them: `total` is
# certification records, `matched` is those resolving to a provider record,
# and `cohort_n` is the live analytic cohort including the nursing-taxonomy
# sensitivity tier.
linkage_total_n <- K$linkage$total
linkage_matched_n <- K$linkage$matched
linkage_matched_pct <- K$linkage$matched_pct
cohort_n <- K$linkage$cohort_n

n_word <- function(x) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
             "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve")
  if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
    if (x >= 1 && x <= length(words)) words[x] else as.character(x)
}

# A NUMBER WORD AT THE START OF A SENTENCE IS STILL THE START OF A SENTENCE.
# n_word() returns lower case because most uses are mid-sentence, and two uses
# in Materials and Methods were not: the rendered manuscript opened sentences
# with "eleven record systems were examined" and "nine sources were compared".
# Capitalizing at the call site is what a copy editor would otherwise do by
# hand on every render.
N_word <- function(x) sub("^(.)", "\\U\\1", n_word(x), perl = TRUE)

pc  <- function(x, d = 1) if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
  sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), x)
cnt <- function(x) if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) "**[PENDING]**" else
  formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
ci_text <- function(x, n, d = 1) {
  ci <- mw_wilson(x, n)
  sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%% (95%% CI, %.", d, "f%%-%.", d, "f%%)"),
          100 * x / n, ci[1], ci[2])
}
sensitivity_text <- function(track, d = 1) {
  lower <- 100 * track$n_accurate / track$n_evaluated
  upper <- 100 * (track$n_accurate + track$n_unresolved) / track$n_evaluated
  sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%-%.", d, "f%%"), lower, upper)
}
```

**Précis:** Selected federal listings of certified nurse-midwives and
certified midwives have high state-board verification yield among resolved
records but disagree about finer-grained administrative location.

## Abstract

**OBJECTIVE:** To examine the accuracy, completeness, and internal
consistency of publicly available databases describing the United States
certified nurse-midwife and certified midwife workforce, and to determine which variables can
support geographic research.

**METHODS:** We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of the 2013 Office of Inspector General evaluation
of federal provider data [@oig2013] for `r cnt(cohort_n)` certified
nurse-midwives and certified midwives drawn from the American Midwifery Certification Board roster
and linked to the National Plan and Provider Enumeration System. State-board
verification yield was assessed for selected listings, and exact
certified-name agreement against the certification-board roster.
Completeness was the proportion of eligible records carrying a value.
Consistency was disagreement in source-to-NPPES comparisons within declared
same-year or current-snapshot overlaps, across `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)`
record systems.

**RESULTS:** Among selected listings resolved to a state-board record, the
board returned a qualifying license outcome -- using live interfaces in three
states and published board files in four more -- for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` of resolved records in the three
live-interface states and `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)`
across all seven, though
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_unresolved, 0)`
of audited records could not be matched to a board record, bounding
seven-state verification yield between
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$worst_case_pct, 0)`
and
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$best_case_pct, 0)`. Of nonqualifying board outcomes,
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_outdated, 1)` were formerly correct and had
gone out of date. Consistency was weaker: the registry and Medicare's
clinician directory disagreed on at least one variable for
`r pc(A$any_inconsistent_2026, 1)` of providers present in both,
concentrated in the finest geographic unit --
`r pc(A$zip_inconsistent, 1)` of ZIP codes but
`r pc(A$state_inconsistent, 1)` of practice states. The versioned
longitudinal audit is reported as exploratory because its input panel differs
from the current panel.

**CONCLUSION:** Practice state showed substantially greater cross-source
agreement than ZIP code. Geographic agreement does not establish accuracy;
state-level analyses require sensitivity to multiple recorded states, and
finer-grained analyses require external location validation.

## Introduction

Research describing the midwifery workforce depends almost entirely on
federal administrative data [@bindman2013npi]. No national registry
records where a certified nurse-midwife practices; investigators
assemble the picture from records created for other purposes, each
capturing a practice address as an administrative by-product. Within
midwifery, identifying the workforce in these files is itself imperfect:
taxonomy codes alone undercount certified midwives, and credential-field
recoding identifies roughly a fifth more of them
[@vanderlaan2023midwives]; the same identification
problem, worse for non-physician clinicians than for physicians, has been
shown nationally for nurse practitioners [@rafalko2025npi].

In May 2013 the Department of Health and Human Services Office of
Inspector General evaluated the two federal systems that establish who a
clinician is and where they practice [@oig2013]. Among the 987,266
providers listed in both, the systems disagreed on at least one variable
for `r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 0)` of providers, and practice location was
the least consistent variable at `r pc(A$oig_zip_benchmark, 1)`. That
evaluation had a gold standard -- a surveyed probability sample -- that
does not exist for this workforce: the certification board is
authoritative for the credential but records no address, and the only
records carrying an address are the records under examination. Two
primary sources do exist for other attributes: state boards of nursing
for licensure status, and the certification board for the certified name.

This study had three objectives: to estimate the accuracy of federal
records describing midwives against independent primary sources; to
quantify completeness and source-to-NPPES consistency across federal and
commercial sources; and to determine which variables are fit for
geographic research on this workforce.

## Methods

### Cohort

The sampling frame was the American Midwifery Certification Board (AMCB)
public verification directory, the national roster of certified nurse-midwives and
certified midwives. The directory publishes certification identity and
status only -- no practice address, city, or state -- and the contact
information the board itself collects is refreshed no more often than
the five-year certification cycle [@vanderlaan2023midwives] and is not
public, so the profession's most complete roster contributes no
location signal to any comparison below.
Certificants were linked to NPPES by name and credential evidence, with linkage decisions
frozen before any analysis in this study was performed. Of `r cnt(linkage_total_n)` certification
records, `r cnt(linkage_matched_n)` (`r pc(linkage_matched_pct, 1)`) resolved
to a provider record through the primary midwifery-taxonomy linkage; a
nursing-taxonomy sensitivity tier adds
`r cnt(cohort_n - linkage_matched_n)` further matches, giving the
analytic cohort of `r cnt(cohort_n)` certificants (Figure 1).
Analyses restricted
to certificants in active status use the narrower tiers below;
each exclusion and its count is diagrammed in Supplemental Figure S8.
Every count in this paper belongs to one of the following tiers:

| Cohort tier | n | Where it is used |
|---|---:|---|
| Certification roster, all statuses | `r cnt(linkage_total_n)` | Sampling frame |
| Resolved to an NPI, primary midwifery taxonomy | `r cnt(linkage_matched_n)` | Linkage rate in this section |
| Nursing-taxonomy sensitivity tier | `r cnt(cohort_n - linkage_matched_n)` | Added to the above |
| Analytic cohort (linkage-eligible, all statuses) | `r cnt(cohort_n)` | Legal-name verification (Table 2); longitudinal comparisons |
| Active certificants | `r cnt(K$exclusion$active_n)` | Figure S8's starting point |
| Active and primary-linked | `r cnt(K$exclusion$active_matched_n)` | Completeness and snapshot comparisons |
| Active, primary-linked, geocoded | `r cnt(K$exclusion$geocoded_n)` | Geographic analyses (Figure S8's endpoint) |
Certification does not imply active practice: roughly a fifth of
certificants report no midwifery employment in the year before
recertification [@vanderlaan2023midwives], so absence from
billing-derived sources is expected for some members rather than
evidence of missing data. This study used only administrative and
publicly available records and was not human subjects research.

![**Figure 1.** Construction of the analytic cohort from the AMCB certification
roster. Included evidence tiers sum to the analytic cohort; mutually exclusive
outcomes outside the cohort are shown separately.](`r fig("federal_database_accuracy_cohort_flow")`)

### Sources

`r N_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems were evaluated, alongside the
certification roster that frames the cohort (Table 1). NPPES
served as the common comparison source, not as a truth standard, because it
assigns the identifier through which every other source is matched.
It instructs providers to update records within 30 days of a change but
neither enforces the update nor verifies that the submitted practice
address is where the provider works [@bindman2013npi].
`r N_word(A$sources_compared_n)` sources were compared pairwise against
it; the full source-by-source matrix, including the pairs that do not
involve the registry, is Supplemental Table S6.
Medicaid, specifically the Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information
System (T-MSIS), was carried as its own classification rather than as a percentage,
because it is the only source with a per-provider-year concordance already
constructed and because reducing enrollment in more than one state within a year to a single
state discards the categories of most interest. Analysis of the enrollment
segments release [@fr2026segments] followed the T-MSIS reporting checklist,
including disclosure of state-level identifiability limits
[@schpero2025taf].

```{r table-sources}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 1. The evaluated record systems, plus the AMCB roster that frames the cohort and serves as a primary source but is not itself an evaluated directory: custodian, role, the years each covers, and the public access point for each, sorted by custodian. The Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System carries a per-provider-year concordance classification -- including enrollment in more than one state at any point in the year -- rather than a single state that could be set against the registry, so its consistency is analyzed separately rather than in Tables 3 and 4."

  open_payments = "Industry-reported payments and transfers of value to covered recipients; nurse-midwives became reportable recipients in program year 2021",
  pecos_revalidation = "Medicare's enrollment, chain, and reassignment records; revalidation carries the practice address on file at enrollment",
  facility_affiliation_ccn = "CMS-published clinician-to-facility affiliation file distributed with the clinician directory",

  "enrollment carries a per-provider-year state concordance, and the 2018-2024",

descr["amcb"] <- paste("The certification board's roster of certified",

if (!is.null(A$coverage_table)) {

  span <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cv, cv$source), function(d) {

    yr_txt <- vapply(runs, function(r)
      if (length(r) == 1) as.character(r) else paste(range(r), collapse = "-"),
      character(1))
    data.frame(

      years = if (length(yrs) == 1) as.character(yrs) else paste(yr_txt, collapse = "; "),
      n_years = length(yrs), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))

  label <- c(
```

Commercial sources were acquired as follows. Healthgrades and Doximity
practice information was retrieved programmatically from each site's
public, login-free profile pages for cohort members. The Trilliant
Health claims-derived practice sites, used only in the rurality
cross-check reported with the record-age results, were read from that
platform's provider directory under the study team's access to it.
The retrieval date, source address, and content hash of every file
each analysis read are recorded in per-artifact provenance manifests
distributed with the analysis code, alongside each source's own vintage
where it publishes one.

### Design

We conducted a conceptual replication of the structure and operational definitions of the Inspector
General's 2013 evaluation [@oig2013], implemented in a package written for
this purpose (`mysteryroster`). The adaptation preserves the evaluation's
three domains and its variable-level definitions, including its three-way
classification of inaccuracy, but differs in population, observation period,
source structure, and reference evidence. Most importantly, the
provider survey that supplied the Office of Inspector General's gold standard was
replaced by primary-source verification against records that exist
independently of the databases being evaluated.

### Accuracy, and the attributes for which it is estimable

Accuracy requires a record that can adjudicate the federal one. The
certification roster can adjudicate the certified name. State-board searches
can establish whether a selected listing resolves to a qualifying board
record, but the analysis does not compare a federal license-status field with
a board-status field. Neither source adjudicates practice location, so the
geographic variables are reported as agreement throughout.

*State-board verification yield* was measured against live state board of nursing records
obtained directly from each state's published licensure system. Three states
publish a machine-readable interface permitting verification of every record
(Colorado, Texas, and Washington); four further states (Connecticut,
Florida, Illinois, and Pennsylvania) were verified from board files
retrieved in October 2026 (Pennsylvania, November 2026). Board records were sought for cohort members
the registry placed in each queried state, so this verification is
scoped to records locatable in those seven states' boards rather than
being a random national sample. Records that could not be matched to a board record were
classified as unresolved. The resolved fraction and extreme sensitivity
bounds are descriptive of this selected search population, not national
license-status accuracy.

*Certified-name agreement* was assessed against the certification board roster.
The roster is authoritative for the name under which a midwife is certified,
not necessarily for the person's current legal name; exact mismatches were
therefore not interpreted as proof that either database was wrong.

Each inaccurate value was classified into the Office of Inspector General's three
subtypes: partially inaccurate, such as a misspelling or transposition;
formerly correct but no longer current; or never correct.

### Completeness

Completeness was the proportion of records eligible for a variable that
carried a populated value, distinguishing a field absent from the extract, a
record missing from the file, and a present record with a null value. Fields
not published by a given source were marked ineligible rather than counted as
incomplete.

### Consistency

Consistency was disagreement between NPPES and another source describing the
same provider. These were source-to-NPPES comparisons rather than all possible
source pairs. For sources with an annual vintage, providers were compared within
the same program year; for sources published only as a current snapshot, the
comparison was against the registry as it stood at extraction. Addresses were normalized following the
Office of Inspector General's appendix. Sources that publish more than
one record per provider-year were reduced to one practice state per
provider-year before comparison, each by a deterministic rule declared
in its extraction script: the registry contributes its annual snapshot's
practice state; Medicare enrollment the state on the revalidation record
at each vintage; Part B and Part D claims the modal billing state (the
state on the most claim rows that year, ties broken deterministically),
with the two claims files treated as one shared-lineage series rather
than two independent sources; and industry payment records the modal
recipient state across payment rows, with the number of states observed
that year retained as a column rather than discarded. Medicaid
enrollment is the one source for which the full set of states is
analytically material, and is classified per provider-year as described
below rather than reduced to a single state. Each source's observation window was declared
before analysis and every input verified for presence, schema and internal
program year, so a missing input failed the analysis rather than silently
narrowing it.

### Record age and resolution

To examine whether disagreement reflected one record going stale, providers were
stratified by the elapsed time since the registry record was last updated, and
ZIP-code disagreement was computed within each stratum. To test whether
disagreements resolve, providers whose registry and Medicare enrollment
records disagreed in 2021 were followed through 2026. A direct persistence
estimate used only providers observed in both systems in 2026; providers absent
from either system were reported as right-censored. Adoption events were
classified separately by whether either source adopted the other's value.

### Analysis

Selected binomial proportions are reported with Wilson score intervals
[@wilson1927inference], which retain nominal coverage at the stratum sizes
used here where the normal-approximation interval does not
[@brown2001binomial]. Because a midwife contributes up to 14 provider-years,
those intervals treat as independent observations that are not; pooled across
each source's window we therefore also report a 400-replicate cluster bootstrap that
resamples midwives rather than provider-years [@efron1979bootstrap;
@field2007bootstrapping], with percentile bounds [@efron1993introduction].
Both intervals are reported for the pooled per-source agreement estimates
in Supplemental Table S7; within a single year each midwife contributes
one provider-year, so per-year strata need no cluster correction.
The temporal trend in agreement was estimated by weighted least squares with
the number of comparable providers as weights, and is reported as a
descriptive slope without a P value: the same midwives contribute to
successive years' agreement rates, so the year-level points are serially
dependent and an independence-based test would overstate the evidence. All analyses were performed
in R.

## Results

### What the sources cover

All `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` evaluated record systems in Table 1 are
reported here (the certification roster, Table 1's remaining row, frames
the cohort and holds no location to evaluate):
`r n_word(A$sources_compared_n)` compared pairwise against the common
comparison source in Tables 3 and 4, that source itself characterized for
completeness in Supplemental Table S1, and Medicaid classified separately below. No single
source covers the full 2007-2026 observation window (Supplemental Figure S1). Four of the `r n_word(A$sources_total_n)`
exist only as a current snapshot and cannot support any longitudinal claim.
Industry payment records begin in program year 2021, the first year in which
certified nurse-midwives were reportable covered recipients.



The structural problem underlying every comparison that follows is shown in
Supplemental Figure S2: the source that is authoritative for the credential holds no
address, and every source that holds an address is either self-reported or
derived from billing.



### State-board verification and certified-name agreement

State-board verification yield is reported for licensure; exact certified-name
agreement is reported against the certification roster. Every geographic figure in this
paper is agreement, not accuracy, and the distinction is not a hedge: a
location on which two databases agree may be wrong in both, and nothing in
this design would detect it.

Among selected national-registry listings that resolved to a board record,
the board returned a qualifying license outcome for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_3$n_definitive)` definitively resolved records in the
three states with machine-readable verification. That analysis left
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_3$n_unresolved)` records unresolved and had sensitivity
bounds of `r sensitivity_text(A$nppes_license_3, 1)`. The corresponding yield was
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_7$n_definitive)` records across all seven states. The
seven-state analysis left `r cnt(A$nppes_license_7$n_unresolved)` registry
records unresolved; treating all unresolved records as inaccurate or all as
accurate produced bounds of `r sensitivity_text(A$nppes_license_7, 1)`. The
subset also present in Medicare enrollment had yields of
`r pc(A$pecos_license_3$pct_accurate, 2)` and
`r pc(A$pecos_license_7$pct_accurate, 2)` respectively. Matching was the
limiting step, not verification: across all seven states,
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_7$n_unresolved)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_license_7$n_evaluated)` registry records
(`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_unresolved, 1)`)
could not be matched to a board record and are unresolved rather than
verified. Counting every unresolved record as inaccurate or as accurate
bounds the seven-state verification yield between
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$worst_case_pct, 1)`
and
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$best_case_pct, 1)`,
so the resolved-record estimate describes only the resolved subset (Table 2).

Among nonqualifying board outcomes across seven states,
`r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_outdated, 1)` were formerly correct and had gone
out of date, `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_typo, 1)` were partially inaccurate,
and `r pc(A$nppes_license_7$pct_never, 1)` had never been correct. In the
three machine-verified states, every nonqualifying outcome was of the formerly
correct type. These categories describe board-search outcomes; they do not
show that a federal license-status field was correct when entered.

Exact certified-name agreement was lower: `r pc(A$nppes_name$pct_accurate, 2)` of
`r cnt(A$nppes_name$n_definitive)` registry records matched the certified
name, and `r pc(A$pecos_name$pct_accurate, 2)` of Medicare enrollment records.
Of the registry mismatches, `r pc(A$nppes_name$pct_typo, 1)` were classified
under the Office of Inspector General scheme as partial mismatches rather than
different people. Such differences may reflect transcription, formatting, or
legitimate name changes; they do not establish which source was current.

```{r table-accuracy}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 2. State-board verification yield among selected federal listings and exact certified-name agreement. Licensure is shown at two search depths -- three states with live board interfaces and seven states after adding four published board files. The producer classifies board-search outcomes; it does not compare a federal license-status field with a board-status field. Unmatched records are unresolved. The certification roster is authoritative for the certified name, not necessarily the name currently used for legal purposes. Geographic tables report agreement rather than verified accuracy."
if (!is.null(A$subtypes_table)) {
  tb <- A$subtypes_table
  # The artifact carries the systems by their acronyms; the manuscript names
  # them, per the journal's preference and so a reader need not decode them.
  db_label <- c("NPPES (2026)" = "National provider registry",
                "PECOS (2026)" = "Medicare enrollment system")
  out <- data.frame(
    `Database` = ifelse(tb$database %in% names(db_label),
                        db_label[tb$database], tb$database),
    `Comparison source` = ifelse(grepl("Name", tb$variable),
                              "Certification board roster",
                              "State boards of nursing"),
    `Attribute` = ifelse(grepl("Name", tb$variable), "Exact certified-name agreement",
                         ifelse(grepl("3 API", tb$variable),
                                "Board verification yield, 3 live-interface states",
                                "Board verification yield, all 7 searched states")),
    `Evaluated` = formatC(as.numeric(tb$n_evaluated), format = "d",
                          big.mark = ","),
    `Unresolved n (%)` = sprintf(
      "%s (%.1f)", formatC(as.numeric(tb$n_unresolved), format = "d",
                           big.mark = ","),
      100 * as.numeric(tb$n_unresolved) / as.numeric(tb$n_evaluated)),
    `Resolved` = formatC(as.numeric(tb$n_definitive), format = "d",
                         big.mark = ","),
    `Qualifying or exact among resolved (%)` =
      sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(tb$pct_accurate_definitive)),
    `95% CI` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(tb)), function(i) {
      z <- mw_wilson(as.numeric(tb$n_accurate[i]), as.numeric(tb$n_definitive[i]))
      sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", z[1], z[2])
    }, character(1)),
    `Worst-best case (%)` = sprintf(
      "%.1f-%.1f",
      100 * as.numeric(tb$n_accurate) / as.numeric(tb$n_evaluated),
      100 * (as.numeric(tb$n_accurate) + as.numeric(tb$n_unresolved)) /
        as.numeric(tb$n_evaluated)),
    `Nonqualifying/mismatched outcomes formerly correct (%)` =
      sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(tb$pct_of_inaccurate_formerly)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out,
                         align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

### Completeness

Completeness was high for the variables that matter geographically. In 2026,
practice state was populated for all but `r pc(A$nppes_state_incomplete, 2)`
of registry records and ZIP code for all but
`r pc(A$nppes_zip_incomplete, 2)`. Completeness was materially worse in the
public clinician directory for non-geographic fields, with telephone number
absent for `r pc(A$dac_phone_incomplete, 1)` and credential for
`r pc(A$dac_cred_incomplete, 1)` of records. One field is absent almost
entirely rather than partially -- the directly reported practice ZIP code
in the 2019 Medicare enrollment extract, null for 99.6% of records -- which is
why practice ZIP code for that source is read from the practice address
instead. For the geographic variables this study compares, completeness is
therefore not the limiting property of these data. Provider-years that leave
a billing source likewise almost always remain visible in the registry, so
source attrition is billing attrition rather than exit from the workforce
(Supplemental Table S4). Completeness also varies geographically inside one
source: in the public Medicaid enrollment file, the share of segments
carrying a provider NPI ranged from `r pc(A$medicaid_npi_pop_min, 1)` in
`r knitr::combine_words(A$medicaid_npi_pop_zero_state_names)` -- whose
files contain no NPI-bearing segment at all -- to `r pc(A$medicaid_npi_pop_max, 1)` in `r A$medicaid_npi_pop_max_state_name`, so a
clinician enrolled only in Oregon Medicaid is unobservable in this source
regardless of record accuracy (Supplemental Figure S6). Field completeness
varies by state in Medicaid files [@samples2025cmc]; CMS's own quality
threshold for missing provider NPIs is 10% [@cms_tmsis_prv_npi], which
`r A$medicaid_npi_pop_n_below_cms` of the `r A$medicaid_npi_pop_n_states`
reporting states and territories do not meet.


### Consistency between databases

Consistency, not accuracy, was the binding constraint. The registry and the
public clinician directory disagreed on at least one variable for
`r pc(A$any_inconsistent_2026, 1)` of `r cnt(A$any_overlap_2026)` providers
present in both, with a mean of
`r sprintf("%.2f", A$mean_inconsistent_vars)` disagreeing variables per
provider. The Office of Inspector General found `r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 1)` on the
same measure across all providers in 2011.

Disagreement was concentrated in the finest geographic unit. Practice ZIP
code disagreed for `r pc(A$zip_inconsistent, 1)` of providers, against the
Office of Inspector General's `r pc(A$oig_zip_benchmark, 1)`, while practice state
disagreed for only `r pc(A$state_inconsistent, 1)` (Figure 2, Table 3). The
same ordering held across the source-to-NPPES comparisons examined.

![**Figure 2.** Disagreement by geographic granularity, against the Office of Inspector
General's 2011 benchmark. The dashed rule marks that benchmark: of the 987,266
providers listed in both federal systems in 2011, 88.6% had a practice-location
ZIP code that did not match between them.](`r fig("address_granularity_vs_oig_benchmark")`)

```{r table-consistency}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 3. Disagreement between the national provider registry and Medicare's public clinician directory, 2026, against the Office of Inspector General's 2011 benchmark."
if (!is.null(A$consistency_table)) {
  cs <- A$consistency_table
  cs <- cs[cs$year == "2026" & cs$source_a == "nppes" &
             cs$source_b == "dac", , drop = FALSE]
  label <- c(practice_zip5 = "Practice location (ZIP code)",
             phone10 = "Telephone number", credential = "Credential",
             full_name = "Full name", gender = "Gender",
             practice_state = "Practice state",
             specialty_code = "Specialty")
  cs <- cs[cs$attribute %in% names(label), , drop = FALSE]
  bm <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(cs$oig_2013_benchmark_inconsistent_pct))
  out <- data.frame(
    Variable = label[cs$attribute],
    `Compared` = formatC(as.numeric(cs$n_compared), format = "d",
                         big.mark = ","),
    `Office of Inspector General 2011 (%)` = ifelse(is.na(bm), "Not reported",
                                          sprintf("%.1f", bm)),
    `Midwifery cohort 2026 (%)` =
      sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(cs$pct_inconsistent_any_shared)),
    `95% CI` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(cs)), function(i) {
      z <- mw_wilson(as.numeric(cs$n_inconsistent_any_shared[i]),
                     as.numeric(cs$n_compared[i]))
      sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", z[1], z[2])
    }, character(1)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out[order(-as.numeric(cs$pct_inconsistent_any_shared)), ],
                         align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

### Record age and the direction of disagreement

Disagreement was not a simple function of staleness. ZIP-code disagreement
was `r pc(A$stale_lt1, 1)` among records updated within the past year,
`r pc(A$stale_1_3, 1)` at one to three years, `r pc(A$stale_3_5, 1)` at three
to five years, and `r pc(A$stale_5p, 1)` beyond five years. The relationship
is U-shaped rather than monotonic: records updated most recently disagree
nearly as often as the most neglected ones. A pattern consistent with this
-- though not directly tested by this design -- is a recent update marking
a recent move that the comparison source has not yet adopted, the
direction of resolution Supplemental Table S3 observes.

An exploratory, versioned longitudinal audit began with
`r cnt(A$disagree_2021_n)` 2021 disagreements, classified
`r cnt(A$observable_2026_n)` as observable in both systems through 2026,
`r cnt(A$persistent_2026_n)` as continuously divergent, and
`r cnt(A$censored_2026_n)` as right-censored. Its provenance pins an older
panel than the current analysis, so these counts describe that historical
run and are not promoted as a current endpoint estimate. Among observed adoption events,
Medicare enrollment adopted the registry's 2021 value after a median of
`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_pecos_adopts_median)` years (IQR
`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_pecos_adopts_p25)`-`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_pecos_adopts_p75)`)
and the registry adopted Medicare enrollment's after a median of
`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_nppes_adopts_median)` years (IQR
`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_nppes_adopts_p25)`-`r sprintf("%g", A$lag_nppes_adopts_p75)`);
adoption ran in both directions, so
the observed resolutions cannot be attributed to a single lagging system
(Supplemental Table S3). Source-level volatility, the year-over-year
persistence of multi-source consensus, and each source's lone-dissent rate
are reported in Supplemental Tables S9-S11.

### Agreement over time

Agreement between the public clinician directory and the registry declined by
`r sprintf("%.2f", A$dac_slope_abs)` percentage points per year across
`r cnt(A$dac_years_n)` years -- a descriptive slope, per Methods -- so the
decline in the most
recent year continues a trend rather than breaking a flat one (Supplemental Figure S3).
Industry payment records and Medicare enrollment records were flat across
their five and six years respectively.



```{r table-agreement}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 4. Practice-state agreement with NPPES, by source and year. Comparable records may exceed the analytic cohort because sources can publish multiple records per clinician; the unique-clinician column shows the distinct NPIs represented."
if (!is.null(A$agreement_table)) {
  ag <- A$agreement_table
  label <- c(dac_physician_compare = "Medicare clinician directory",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records",
             pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             facility_affiliation_ccn = "Hospital affiliation",
             medicare_claims = "Medicare claims (Parts B and D)",
             healthgrades = "Healthgrades", doximity = "Doximity",
             state_boards_of_nursing = "State boards of nursing",
             cms_ndh_fhir = "National directory of healthcare providers")
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = label[ag$source],
    Period = ifelse(grepl("^[0-9]{4}$", ag$year), ag$year,
                    sub(" \\(.*$", "", ag$year)),
    Basis = ifelse(ag$comparison_basis == "same_year", "Same year",
                   "Current snapshot"),
    `Comparable records` = formatC(as.numeric(ag$n_comparable), format = "d",
                       big.mark = ","),
    `Unique clinicians` = formatC(as.numeric(ag$n_npis_comparable), format = "d",
                       big.mark = ","),
    `Agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ag$pct_agree)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

### One classified Medicaid provider-year in six has an any-time multistate class

Under the historical classification, `r pc(A$medicaid_multistate_pct, 1)` of provider-years
outside the "not observed" category in the
Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System (T-MSIS) carried
enrollment in more than one state at some point in the enrollment year --
an any-time measure, not enrollment in several states on one date. This
denominator includes indeterminate classifications and is not the count with
qualifying enrollment evidence. On a common snapshot date within the year,
among comparable pairs, the multistate share is
`r pc(A$medicaid_multistate_snapshot_pct, 1)`, so the any-time rule adds
`r sprintf("%.1f", A$medicaid_multistate_anytime_pct - A$medicaid_multistate_snapshot_pct)`
percentage points of apparent multistate enrollment. This demonstrates that a scoring
rule requiring one state per provider-year can manufacture disagreement; it
does not mean that every multistate record would be misclassified. T-MSIS was
therefore classified per provider-year rather than reduced to one assigned
state.

Across `r A$medicaid_years` T-MSIS contributed
`r cnt(A$medicaid_total_n)` provider-years, of which
`r cnt(A$medicaid_observed_n)` were outside the "not observed" class; this
historical denominator is not synonymous with observed qualifying enrollment.
`r cnt(A$medicaid_concordant_n)` were concordant with the registry on a single
state and a further `r cnt(A$medicaid_multistate_concordant_n)` were
concordant through enrollment in more than one state during the year, meaning the
registry's state was among those a midwife was enrolled in.
These classification counts arise from the enrollment-classification artifact.
The separate scoring-rule analysis in Supplemental Table S5 contains
`r cnt(A$medicaid_comparable_npi_years)` provider-years because it uses all
comparable NPI-year state sets rather than the classification artifact's
restricted observation universe; the two denominators should not be pooled.

### Multistate enrollment as a source of apparent disagreement

A portion of the disagreement between sources is not error. Scoring Medicaid
enrollment by whether a state is among those in which a midwife is
enrolled at any point in the year, rather than by whether it equals a single state
selected for her, raised agreement with the registry from
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_pct, 1)` (95% CI
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_ci_low, 1)` to
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_ci_high, 1)`) to
`r pc(A$medicaid_membership_pct, 1)` (95% CI
`r pc(A$medicaid_membership_ci_low, 1)` to
`r pc(A$medicaid_membership_ci_high, 1)`) on the same
`r cnt(A$medicaid_comparable_npi_years)` comparable provider-years, a paired
gain of `r sprintf("%.1f", A$medicaid_membership_pct - A$medicaid_equality_pct)`
percentage points (provider-cluster bootstrap 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.1f", A$medicaid_diff_ci_low)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", A$medicaid_diff_ci_high)`). The gain is nonnegative by
construction, since a state equal to the modal pick is always in the enrolled
set.
No underlying record changed; only the question did (Supplemental
Table S5). Commercial insurer
directories show the same mechanism: practice-address consistency rose
from 27.9% to 84.8% when only physicians practicing at a single location
were counted [@butala2023directories].

Multistate enrollment occurs among midwives who
appear in Medicaid at all (Supplemental Figure S4); enrollment out of
state adds credentialing requirements [@macpac2026enrollment]. The data do
not establish whether the states were used for cross-border clinical
practice, telehealth, sequential enrollment, or administrative reasons.
Enrollment is not observed delivery or verified practice location.



Consistent with this, providers licensed in more than one state accounted for
a disproportionate share of cross-source disagreement (Supplemental Figure S5).
Unanimous agreement likewise falls as more sources report a state for the
same provider-year (Supplemental Table S2), and agreement with the registry
varies widely by the provider's state (Supplemental Figure S7).



## Discussion

### Principal findings

Three findings organize the results. First, among selected federal listings
that resolved to a state-board record, the board returned a qualifying
outcome for
`r pc(A$nppes_license_3$pct_accurate, 0)` to
`r pc(A$pecos_license_3$pct_accurate, 0)` of resolved records. The limit is
the roughly two in five seven-state records that no board record could be
matched to, the selected search population, and the absence of a direct
comparison between federal and board license-status fields (Table 2).
Second, cross-source consistency is limiting. Populated
records maintained on different schedules diverge, concentrated in the
finest geographic unit, replicating the
2013 ordering thirteen years later at similar
magnitudes. Third, the historical follow-up shows adoption in both directions
and substantial censoring, but a cohort-bound current endpoint remains to be
produced before persistence is treated as a headline estimate.

### Implications for workforce and access research

These results draw a boundary through the
geographic hierarchy. Practice
state had substantially greater cross-source agreement than ZIP code in the
tested comparison --
agreement, not verified accuracy, and sources that share lineage or
selection can agree and still be wrong together; ZIP
code had materially lower agreement. This study does not establish a
universal threshold at which fine-grained analysis becomes impossible. Licensure
files show the same
hazard: one statewide study matched nurse-practitioner board addresses
to employment in 5% of cases, registry addresses in 64%
[@bell2018licensure].

Timeliness inverts a common assumption: where sources and the registry
disagreed on practice state across transitions, Medicare claims held the
registry's eventual value first in `r pc(A$claims_lead_partb_pct, 1)` of
Part B and `r pc(A$claims_lead_partd_pct, 1)` of Part D disagreements --
roughly three in five. The ordering does not observe a practice change or
establish which value was correct. In a commercial-reporting source, of the `r cnt(L$state_disc_2022_n)`
practice-state disagreements between Open Payments and the registry in
2022, `r pc(L$state_b_adopts_pct, 1)` resolved by the registry later adopting
the Open Payments state within four years. This sequence is consistent with
the payment file carrying the later registry value first, but it does not
observe a visit, a move date, or truth.

Billing visibility is itself regime-dependent. In states that condition
midwifery practice on physician collaboration or supervision
[@Ranchoff2020scope], many of them in the South, services a midwife
furnishes may be billed under the collaborating physician's identifier,
so her own NPI need never appear in a claims file at all;
under-identification of non-physician clinicians in claims-derived data
is documented beyond midwifery [@rafalko2025npi]. A certificant
invisible to billing is not absent from the workforce -- she is absent
from one observation channel -- and no single system observes every
channel. That asymmetry, not convenience, is why this study consulted
`r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems, besides the certification
roster itself, rather than nominating any
one of them as authoritative: no single query of any single database
answers where a midwife practices. The directories
researchers reach for are snapshots that cannot express
lag. A study prioritizing recent billing location may prefer claims-derived
sources; one prioritizing a broad denominator may prefer the registry, while
recognizing that neither source directly establishes current practice.

The boundary applies to access-to-care inference. One Medicaid
provider-year in six carried enrollment in more than one
state during the year; scoring that file by a single assigned state created additional
apparent disagreement (agreement rose from
`r pc(A$medicaid_equality_pct, 1)` to `r pc(A$medicaid_membership_pct, 1)`
on identical data). For a workforce holding multiple state licenses,
"the practice state" is partly an artifact of the question asked.

| Research purpose | Preferred source or approach | Main caution |
|:---|:---|:---|
| National workforce denominator | NPPES-based registry cohort | May include clinicians who are not currently practicing |
| Recent billing location | Recent claims | Excludes nonbilling practice and may reflect billing rather than worksite address |
| State-level distribution | NPPES with multistate sensitivity analysis | Agreement is not verified accuracy |
| City- or ZIP-code-level access | External validation or multisource adjudication | High cross-source disagreement |
| Licensure status | Live state board record | Availability and machine readability vary by state |

Table 5. Practical interpretation of the sources for common workforce research
purposes. These are design recommendations, not claims that any source is a
truth standard.

### Comparison with previous studies

This study conceptually replicates and extends. The Office of Inspector
General's 2013 evaluation established the accuracy--completeness--consistency
framework, with a surveyed provider sample as the reference standard
[@oig2013]; sibling evaluations had already found stale terminated
relationships in the Medicare enrollment extract, missing elements in
industry payment records, and improving but uneven Medicaid submission
completeness [@oig2009pecos; @oig2018openpayments; @gao2021tmsis]. Subsequent
work comparing national physician sampling
frames, licensure records, and commercial directories documented
discrepancies in clinician addresses and specialty classifications
[@desroches2015sampling; @bell2018licensure; @resneck2014dermatology;
@butala2024directory]; a national comparison of five
major insurer directories found consistent practice-address information
for only 27.9% of physicians listed in more than one directory
[@butala2023directories]; one re-survey found 44.8% of inaccurate
listings still wrong months later [@haeder2024persistence], and the
regulator's audit found half of Medicare Advantage directory
locations inaccurate [@cms2018directory]. Within
midwifery, taxonomy alone undercounts certified midwives and credential
fields improve identification, but that work addressed identification,
not the validity of practice addresses [@vanderlaan2023midwives].

Against this literature, the consistency findings replicate almost
exactly -- the same concentration in ZIP code, the same variable
ordering, and lower any-variable disagreement than the
`r pc(A$oig_any_benchmark, 0)` found across all providers in 2011, which
may reflect a more uniformly enumerated workforce rather than
improvement. The extension is a certification-defined cohort across
`r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems, external verification where
a primary source exists, and longitudinal resolution data consistent with
the 1.2% update-lag finding: most disagreement persists for years.

### Strengths and limitations

The strengths are the cohort and the design: a certification-board frame
linked by a frozen, fully-accounted matching procedure, and comparisons
computed only within declared, content-verified observation windows --
every figure compares records within declared source-specific units and
observation windows. Linkage evidence tiers and unresolved records are retained
in the frozen linkage artifacts; the cohort counts in Methods make the
midwifery-taxonomy and nursing-taxonomy tiers explicit.

The limitations bound what can be claimed. Four of the
`r n_word(A$sources_total_n)` record systems exist only as snapshots, so
their quality over time is not measurable.
Practice-location accuracy is not estimable: every geographic figure is
agreement, and a location on which two databases agree may be wrong in
both. Agreement comparisons weight by published records, so multi-record
sources count providers repeatedly. Agreement between sources sharing
upstream lineage -- Medicare Part B and Part D claims, Medicare
enrollment and the directory it feeds -- is within a family, not
independent corroboration. That ceiling is measurable: across the
`r n_word(A$move_corrob_transitions_n)` state-to-state move transitions
examined, once shared lineage is discounted Open Payments is the only
remaining candidate for a second, independent witness, and independent
corroboration of a mover's destination never exceeded
`r pc(A$move_corrob_indep_max_pct, 1)` of movers in any transition --
the source set cannot independently verify where a confirmed mover
went, for any year.

Although location accuracy is not estimable, the character of a
geographic disagreement is. In a cross-check outside the Table 1
systems, each cohort member's registered NPPES practice address was
compared against the practice site where a commercial claims aggregate
(Trilliant Health) observes their care, with each address assigned a
Rural-Urban Continuum class (metropolitan, nonmetropolitan adjacent, or
nonmetropolitan remote). Among the `r cnt(A$dist_diff_band_coords_n)`
midwives whose two addresses carry different classes and have
coordinates for both, none lie within `r round(A$dist_mi_10km)` miles
(10 km) of each other, `r pc(A$dist_diff_band_ge40km_pct, 0)` are
`r round(A$dist_mi_40km)` miles (40 km) or more apart, and
`r cnt(A$dist_diff_band_ge250km_n)` are `r round(A$dist_mi_250km)` miles
(250 km) or more apart; a further `r cnt(A$dist_same_band_ge250km_n)`
midwives match on class while the two addresses sit
`r round(A$dist_mi_250km)` miles or more apart. A rurality disagreement
is therefore two genuinely different places -- consistent with a
registration address maintained on an enrollment clock while care is
delivered elsewhere -- rather than noise at a county boundary, and a
county-level location assigned from either source alone inherits that
gap. Neither source is ground truth and the claims observation window is
not documented, so these distances characterize the disagreement without
adjudicating it.

### Conclusion

Federal and commercial databases showed substantially higher agreement on
practice state than on finer geography, but agreement does not establish
geographic accuracy. Divergence was persistent and is consistent with records
maintained on different schedules. State-level estimates may be defensible
with multistate sensitivity analyses; city- and ZIP-code-level analyses
require external validation. The registry offers a broad denominator and
billing-derived sources offer more recent activity signals, but neither is a
truth standard; study design should choose the property the question needs.

```{r table-source-count-agreement}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S2. Practice-state agreement as a function of the number of sources reporting a state in the same provider-year, in the style of the cross-directory comparison of Butala et al. Unanimous agreement requires every reporting source to record the same state; pairwise agreement is the share of source-pairs that agree. Unanimous agreement declines as more sources report, mirroring the dose-response reported for commercial insurer directories."
if (!is.null(A$source_count_table)) {
  sc <- A$source_count_table
  out <- data.frame(
    `Sources reporting a practice state` = sc$n_sources_reporting,
    `Provider-years` = formatC(as.numeric(sc$n_provider_years), format = "d",
                               big.mark = ","),
    `All sources agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
                                      as.numeric(sc$pct_unanimous_agreement)),
    `Source-pairs agreeing (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
                                          as.numeric(sc$pct_pairwise_agreement)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-resolution-disposition}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S3. Disposition of provider-years on which a source and the national provider registry held discordant practice states, measured at the next observation, in the style of the follow-up taxonomy of Haeder and Zhu. Counts and shares pool every paired transition in each source's observation window rather than a single base-year cohort; the paired series begins in 2013 for the Medicaid and Medicare sources and in 2021 for enrollment revalidation and industry payments. 'Source adopted registry' and 'registry adopted source' are the two directions of resolution, and the residual is the share whose next observation is missing because the provider-year left observation. The four shares sum to 100 by construction."
if (!is.null(A$resolution_table)) {
  rs <- A$resolution_table
  label <- c(pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             medicare_part_b = "Medicare Part B claims",
             medicare_part_d = "Medicare Part D claims",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records",
             medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment (T-MSIS)")[rs$source_b]
  # DEBT D14 items 3 and 4, fixed here rather than in the caption.
  #
  # The `Base year` column is gone. Every count and share in this row pools the
  # source's whole window: b_adopts_a_at_t1_pct is b_adopts_a_at_t1_n over
  # n_discordant_at_t, which is 23,315 paired transitions for Medicaid where
  # the base-year cohort disc_base_n is 1,316. A reader given a base year
  # beside a pooled count reads the pooled count as a base-year count. The
  # base-year cohort has its own follow-up columns in the artifact
  # (disc_base_n with the _multi_ shares); reporting it is a different table,
  # not a relabelling of this one, so the window is stated in the caption
  # instead.
  #
  # `Both moved (%)` is gone for a different reason: both_move_together_at_t1
  # counts provider-years that AGREED at t and moved together at t+1, a
  # sub-count of n_concordant_at_t, and it was divided by n_discordant_at_t.
  # Over the wrong group the open_payments row summed to 114.5%. The residual
  # below is what that column was reaching for and is in the right group: the
  # discordant provider-years whose next observation does not exist.
  resid <- 100 - (as.numeric(rs$persistent_discordant_at_t1_pct) +
                  as.numeric(rs$b_adopts_a_at_t1_pct) +
                  as.numeric(rs$a_reverts_to_b_at_t1_pct))
  stopifnot(all(resid >= -1e-6))
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(label), rs$source_b, label),
    `Discordant (n)` = formatC(as.numeric(rs$n_discordant_at_t), format = "d",
                               big.mark = ","),
    `Still discordant (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$persistent_discordant_at_t1_pct)),
    `Source adopted registry (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$b_adopts_a_at_t1_pct)),
    `Registry adopted source (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      as.numeric(rs$a_reverts_to_b_at_t1_pct)),
    `Left observation (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", resid),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-persistence-denominators}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S4. Where a provider-year goes by the following year, aggregated across the years of each source's window for which a following year exists in that source and in the national provider registry. Each source's last observed year is excluded: there is no next year to be followed into, so every provider-year in it would count as lost by arithmetic rather than by attrition, and a row whose next year falls past the registry's last year cannot distinguish absence from the registry from a registry that has not been observed yet. A provider who leaves a billing source is rarely leaving the workforce: most remain visible in the national provider registry, so source attrition is billing attrition rather than exit from practice. Same-state and different-state shares are computed among provider-years re-observed in the same source; the leavers' registry-visibility share is computed among provider-years absent from the source at the next observation. The registry itself is omitted because persistence in it and visibility in it cannot be distinguished."
if (!is.null(A$persistence_table)) {
  ps <- A$persistence_table
  ps <- ps[ps$source != "nppes", , drop = FALSE]
  label <- c(nppes = "National provider registry",
             pecos_revalidation = "Medicare enrollment revalidation",
             medicare_claims = "Medicare claims (Parts B and D)",
             medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment (T-MSIS)",
             open_payments = "Industry payment records")[ps$source]
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(label), ps$source, label),
    `Observed (n)` = formatC(ps$n_observed, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `In source next year (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_followed_source / ps$n_observed),
    `Same state (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_same_state / ps$n_followed_source),
    `Different state (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_changed_state / ps$n_followed_source),
    `Left source (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_lost_from_source / ps$n_observed),
    `Leavers still in registry (%)` = sprintf("%.1f",
      100 * ps$n_lost_source_but_in_nppes / ps$n_lost_from_source),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out[order(-ps$n_observed), ],
                         align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-set-membership}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S5. Medicaid enrollment versus the national provider registry on identical provider-years under two scoring rules, adopting the two-universe column design of Butala et al., who reported directory consistency for all physicians and for the restricted universe of single-location physicians side by side. Equality requires the registry state to equal the single state the file would assign; membership requires it to be among the states in which the provider was enrolled at any point in the year. The gap between the two columns is apparent disagreement manufactured by the scoring rule, not error in the underlying records."
if (!is.null(A$setm_table)) {
  getq <- function(lbl) {
    v <- A$setm_table$value[A$setm_table$quantity == lbl]
    if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(v)
  }
  out <- data.frame(
    `Scoring rule` = c(
      "Equality: registry state must equal the single assigned state",
      "Membership: registry state among the enrolled states"),
    `Provider-years` = formatC(
      rep(getq("comparable NPI-years vs NPPES"), 2), format = "d",
      big.mark = ","),
    `Agreement with registry (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", c(
      getq("agreement, equality with the modal pick (%)"),
      getq("agreement, membership of the enrolled set (%)"))),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-pairwise-matrix}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S6. Practice-state agreement for every source pair, not only each source against the registry hub. The longitudinal tier counts provider-years across the pair's overlapping observation window; the snapshot tier compares the pair at its single common vintage, so a pair appearing in both tiers answers two different questions rather than repeating one. Pairs marked with an asterisk share upstream lineage -- Part B and Part D claims, or Medicare enrollment and the directory family it feeds -- so their agreement is family resemblance rather than independent corroboration. Pairs marked with a dagger involve the state boards of nursing: board records were harvested only for cohort members whose NPPES practice state matched the queried board, so state-level agreement in these rows is conditioned on one side of the comparison and overstates agreement by construction; they are reported for completeness, not as independent confirmation. 'Of cohort (%)' reports each snapshot comparison's comparable providers as a share of the analytic cohort, so a high agreement percentage on a thin, selected overlap cannot read the same as one on broad coverage; longitudinal rows span windows of different lengths, so their selectivity is carried by the comparable provider-year count rather than a single shared denominator."
if (!is.null(A$pairwise_matrix_table)) {
  pm <- A$pairwise_matrix_table
  lbl <- c(nppes = "NPPES",
           medicare_part_b = "Medicare Part B claims",
           medicare_part_d = "Medicare Part D claims",
           pecos_revalidation = "PECOS revalidation",
           open_payments = "Open Payments",
           medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment",
           dac_physician_compare = "CMS clinician directory",
           cms_ndh_fhir = "CMS NDH directory",
           facility_affiliation_ccn = "Facility affiliations",
           healthgrades = "Healthgrades",
           doximity = "Doximity",
           state_boards_of_nursing = "State boards of nursing")
  nm <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(lbl[x]), x, unname(lbl[x]))
  board <- pm$source_a == "state_boards_of_nursing" |
    pm$source_b == "state_boards_of_nursing"
  out <- data.frame(
    Tier = ifelse(pm$tier == "longitudinal_provider_years",
                  "Longitudinal (provider-years)",
                  "Snapshot (common vintage)"),
    Pair = paste0(nm(pm$source_a), " vs ", nm(pm$source_b),
                  ifelse(pm$shared_lineage, "*", ""),
                  ifelse(board, "†", "")),
    Comparable = formatC(as.numeric(pm$n_comparable), format = "d",
                         big.mark = ","),
    `Of cohort (%)` = ifelse(
      pm$tier == "longitudinal_provider_years", "--",
      sprintf("%.1f", 100 * as.numeric(pm$n_comparable) / cohort_n)),
    `Agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(pm$pct_agree)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-agreement-ci}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S7. Pooled practice-state agreement with the registry for the longitudinal billing-derived sources, with both interval constructions the Methods specify: the Wilson interval, which treats provider-years as independent, and the provider-cluster bootstrap interval, which resamples midwives rather than provider-years. The final column is the bootstrap interval width divided by the Wilson interval width; it is a width ratio, not a variance-ratio design effect."
if (!is.null(A$agreement_ci_table)) {
  ci <- A$agreement_ci_table
  lbl <- c(medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment",
           medicare_claims = "Medicare Part B and Part D claims",
           open_payments = "Open Payments",
           pecos_revalidation = "PECOS revalidation")
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(lbl[ci$source]), ci$source, unname(lbl[ci$source])),
    `Provider-years` = formatC(as.numeric(ci$n_npi_years), format = "d",
                               big.mark = ","),
    Providers = formatC(as.numeric(ci$n_npis), format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Agree (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ci$pct_agree)),
    `Wilson 95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", as.numeric(ci$wilson_low),
                              as.numeric(ci$wilson_high)),
    `Cluster bootstrap 95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f-%.1f",
                                         as.numeric(ci$boot_low),
                                         as.numeric(ci$boot_high)),
    `CI width ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(ci$design_effect)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  out <- out[order(out$Source), ]
  style_manuscript_table(out,
                         align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-censoring-audit}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S8. Mutually exclusive 2021-2026 disposition of providers whose registry and Medicare enrollment practice states disagreed in 2021. Persistence in 2026 is estimated among providers observed in both systems; right-censored providers remain in the starting-cohort accounting but not the persistence denominator."
if (!is.null(A$censoring_table)) {
  ca <- A$censoring_table
  out <- data.frame(
    Disposition = sub("^[0-9]+\\. ", "", ca$longitudinal_disposition),
    Providers = formatC(as.numeric(ca$n_clinicians), format = "d",
                        big.mark = ","),
    `Starting cohort (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ca$pct_of_all_892)),
    `Observed through 2026 (%)` = ifelse(
      is.na(as.numeric(ca$pct_of_728_uncensored)), "Not applicable",
      sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ca$pct_of_728_uncensored))),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-churn}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S9. Year-over-year volatility of each source's own practice-state value (churn): among consecutive-year transitions within one source, the share whose state changed, with a Wilson 95% interval. Churn measures how often a source rewrites itself, independent of whether either value is right; a stale source and a noisy source fail differently, and this column separates them."
if (!is.null(A$churn_table)) {
  ch <- A$churn_table
  lbl <- c(nppes = "NPPES",
           medicare_part_b = "Medicare Part B claims",
           medicare_part_d = "Medicare Part D claims",
           medicare_claims = "Medicare Part B and Part D claims",
           pecos_revalidation = "PECOS revalidation",
           open_payments = "Open Payments",
           medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment")
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(lbl[ch$source]), ch$source, unname(lbl[ch$source])),
    `Consecutive-year transitions` = formatC(as.numeric(ch$n_transitions),
                                             format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `State changed` = formatC(as.numeric(ch$n_changed), format = "d",
                              big.mark = ","),
    `Churn (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(ch$pct)),
    `95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f-%.1f", as.numeric(ch$ci_low),
                       as.numeric(ch$ci_high)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  out <- out[order(-as.numeric(ch$pct)), ]
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-tier-flow}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S10. Does multi-source consensus persist year over year, or churn? Each row counts midwives moving from one consensus tier (unanimous, majority, split) to another across consecutive years, 2021-2025, within the cohort for which all four comparison sources are present in every year. Diagonal rows (same tier both years) are stability; off-diagonal rows are consensus churn."
if (!is.null(A$tier_flow_table)) {
  tf <- A$tier_flow_table
  out <- data.frame(
    `Years` = paste(tf$year_from, "to", tf$year_to),
    `Tier at start` = tf$tier1,
    `Tier at end` = tf$tier2,
    Midwives = formatC(as.numeric(tf$n), format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    check.names = FALSE)
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r"))
}
```

```{r table-odd-one-out}
#| tbl-cap: "Supplemental Table S11. Lone-dissent rate per source: among identifier-years where three or more sources report a practice state and all others agree, how often this source is the single dissenter. A tied split with no majority is not a lone dissent. A high rate marks the source the comparison set most often has to outvote."
if (!is.null(A$odd_one_out_table)) {
  oo <- A$odd_one_out_table
  lbl <- c(nppes = "NPPES",
           medicare_part_b = "Medicare Part B claims",
           medicare_part_d = "Medicare Part D claims",
           pecos_revalidation = "PECOS revalidation",
           open_payments = "Open Payments",
           medicaid_enrollment = "Medicaid enrollment",
           dac_physician_compare = "CMS clinician directory",
           cms_ndh_fhir = "CMS NDH directory",
           facility_affiliation_ccn = "Facility affiliations",
           healthgrades = "Healthgrades",
           doximity = "Doximity",
           state_boards_of_nursing = "State boards of nursing")
  out <- data.frame(
    Source = ifelse(is.na(lbl[oo$source]), oo$source, unname(lbl[oo$source])),
    `Eligible identifier-years` = formatC(as.numeric(oo$n_eligible),
                                          format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Lone dissents` = formatC(as.numeric(oo$n_odd_one_out), format = "d",
                              big.mark = ","),
    `Lone-dissent rate (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * as.numeric(oo$odd_rate)),
    check.names = FALSE)
  out <- out[order(-as.numeric(oo$odd_rate)), ]
  style_manuscript_table(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
}
```
